As demand for artificial intelligence continues to reshape the global data landscape, investors are weighing the explosive growth of Credo Technology Group (NASDAQ:CRDO) against the established dominance of Marvell Technology (NASDAQ:MRVL).

Credo specializes in energy-efficient connectivity for high-speed networks, focusing on specific bottlenecks in hyperscale data centers. Marvell offers a more diverse range of semiconductor solutions covering storage, optical, and computing needs across the entire networking ecosystem. Comparing these two reveals a choice between a high-growth specialist and a diversified infrastructure giant.

The case for Credo Technology Group

Credo focuses on designing high-speed copper and optical interconnect solutions that facilitate massive data movements within cloud networks. The company primarily serves blue chip hyperscalers and equipment manufacturers, with high-profile partnerships including Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) and Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT). Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, as nearly 90% of revenue in its latest annual report came from just 10 customers.

In the 12 months ended Aug. 1, 2026, revenue reached close to $1.6 billion, representing explosive growth of approximately 165.1% compared to the prior period. This rapid scaling helped the company generate a net income of roughly $538.3 million during that time frame. The resulting net margin of 33.8% highlights how effectively the company is translating its semiconductor stock sales into actual earnings as it expands.

As of its May 2026 balance sheet, the current ratio, which measures whether a company can cover its short-term debts with short-term assets, is 10.2x. The debt-to-equity ratio is 0.0x, indicating a balance sheet with no total debt relative to shareholder equity. In the fiscal year ended May 2, 2026, free cash flow was approximately $407.0 million. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 39.3% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back to cash flow in the cash flow statement.

The case for Marvell Technology

Marvell Technology provides the foundational hardware required to move, store, and process data across cloud and automotive markets. The company has a strong focus on the data center segment, which is increasingly driven by demand for custom silicon and high-speed networking. Marvell also maintains high customer concentration, as its top 10 customers accounted for roughly 82% of its revenue in its latest annual report.

Key Takeaways

Oracle sold $20 billion of stock and bonds days after capping new capital-market funding at that amount through fiscal 2030.

Bloomberg reported that Microsoft is winding down a 2023 deal to rent AI computing from Oracle on older Nvidia chips.

Cloud infrastructure revenue rose 121% last quarter, but free cash flow was negative $5 billion as data center spending ran ahead.

Oracle's fiscal second-quarter report, expected in December, must show cloud revenue growth of 65% to 71% to match guidance.

Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) has crammed a quarter's worth of news into two weeks. On November 2, it priced $20 billion of new stock and bonds. Four days later, Bloomberg reported that Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ) is winding down a deal to rent AI computing from Oracle.

Then the mood flipped. Strong results from CoreWeave (CRWV:NASDAQ) sparked a rally in AI cloud stocks on November 11, and Oracle rose with the group. It is also preparing to offer chips from Alphabet (GOOGL:NASDAQ) in its cloud starting in 2027.

Before that bounce, Oracle sat among AI cloud names down 32% to 48% this year. The open question is whether its funding plan and $664 billion backlog hold up as big buyers rethink their AI capacity.

Funding capped, then fully tapped

Oracle set this up at its October 28 investor day. It capped new capital-market funding through fiscal 2030 at $20 billion, excluding refinancing.

Five days later, it used the whole cap in one go:

86.2 million new shares at $116 each, for about $9.9 billion in net proceeds

$10 billion of senior notes

Both deals closed on November 4

That clears a funding overhang. However, it also adds dilution and fresh interest costs to a balance sheet already carrying heavy debt…

Oracle (ORCL): total debt, quarterly, $ billions, Q1 FY2025–Q1 FY2027 (TIKR)

Then came Microsoft. According to Bloomberg, the company has been switching off rented Oracle capacity since it declined to renew. The 2023 deal ran AI features in Bing on an older generation of Nvidia chips.

Oracle answered fast, and a spokesperson told Reuters that demand for its AI infrastructure "remains strong, including for earlier-generation GPUs."

The backlog still carries the case

Oracle never disclosed the Microsoft deal's terms. Yet its newer signings tell a fuller story. In the fiscal first quarter ended August 31, it booked more than $30 billion of new AI cloud contracts. Remaining performance obligations reached $664 billion, up $209 billion from a year earlier.

US stocks edged lower Thursday, snapping a rebound that had lifted the S&P 500 1.3% a day earlier. The S&P 500 fell 0.35% to 7,592.40, the Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.36% to 52,297.09, and the Nasdaq Composite lost 0.39% to 25,366.09, Yahoo Finance reported, as bond yields rose. Traders weighed hot inflation data, the Federal Reserve's next move and higher oil prices.

Hot Inflation Keeps the Fed in Focus

The week's moves have been shaped by interest rates. Tuesday's hotter-than-expected inflation report convinced traders that the Federal Reserve will raise rates next month, Reuters said. According to CME FedWatch, investors fully price in a hike of at least 25 basis points, with a 13.2% chance of a 50-basis-point move. Several Fed officials have said they are open to a more aggressive path, and Wall Street analysts have raised their forecasts for more and bigger hikes, Yahoo Finance said.

Wednesday's rebound showed how quickly sentiment can swing. The S&P 500 gained 1.3% and the Nasdaq Composite 1.6% after results from an AI cloud company eased worries about the durability of the artificial intelligence trade, Reutersreported, with advancing stocks outnumbering decliners by 1.3 to 1 on the NYSE. The Treasury market was closed for Veterans Day, so bond traders could react only on Thursday.

Oil Adds to the Uncertainty

Thursday brought another pressure point. Oil prices climbed after the president said he was no longer interested in a deal with Iran, the Associated Press reported, which complicates the inflation outlook. Higher energy costs feed into the same inflation numbers the Fed is fighting. Even so, the S&P 500 finished with a modest loss and is up 2.9% for the week.

Retail investors are watching the same swings closely, and Reddit threads tend to cluster around names where the gap between price and analyst expectations looks widest. That gap deserves some care. An average price target is a twelve-month estimate pulled from sell-side analysts, it is often revised after earnings, and a handful of outliers can skew the mean. Because upside is measured against the current share price, a sharp drop widens it overnight, while a rally shrinks it just as fast. Wall Street's AI trade just had one of its worst weeks in years. Politics and inflation hit it at the same time. The Nasdaq Composite posted its deepest one-day drop since April 2025 last week, after Democrats swept the midterm elections and investors began weighing tougher scrutiny of AI and limits on data center construction. The Cboe Volatility Index climbed to a seven-month high the same day.

Why the AI Selloff Hit Chip and Data Center Stocks So Hard

Stocks first cheered the election. They closed sharply higher the day after the vote because the result cleared up political uncertainty. Then chipmakers and data center operators fell, even as the biggest, cash-rich AI spenders rose. A slower buildout eases cash demands on the companies doing the spending, but it squeezes the operators and suppliers whose growth depends on fast construction.

Scott Chronert, head of US equity strategy at Citi Research, said a change in the pace of the data center buildout changes the basic path for many of those suppliers. Our list of oversold AI stocks where Wall Street analysts see 50% upside or more covers more of the group.

Hot Inflation Puts the Fed Back in Focus

Inflation added a second worry. The Labor Department said consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, a third straight gain of 0.4% or more. Economists polled by Reuters had expected 0.3%. Markets now fully price in a Federal Reserve rate increase of at least 25 basis points in December, up from 84% a day earlier, according to CME FedWatch.

Fed Governor Christopher Waller said the central bank should raise rates in December even if inflation had cooled. He said a half-point move should be considered if the picture worsened. Jason Ware, chief investment officer at Albion Financial Group, said investors began to wonder whether the Fed worried more about inflation than they did, and sold some stocks.

The rout wiped out trillions of dollars in market value and clouded the outlook for a global economy the AI boom has been supporting. Readers following the chip side of the trade can find more names in our list of the best semiconductor stocks to buy for the next decade. Ahead of the Fed's December meeting, traders expect about two more quarter-point increases in total this cycle, according to LSEG data.

Advanced Micro Devices' (AMD) stock looks poised to revisit its all-time highs. The market has already bought into its growth story. Now, the next opportunity may lie in how much of that growth turns into profits. After a triple-digit gain in 2026, the stock has pulled back from its October record highs, but the fundamentals help explain much of that rally.

In its third-quarter earnings report, released on November 3, the Santa Clara, California-based chipmaker reported that its Data Center revenue nearly doubled, along with a great improvement in margins.

The most interesting part may still be ahead. With much greater visibility into 2027, I believe the market still underestimates the company's earnings growth potential. That's why I remain bullish, even with an already demanding valuation.

AMD's Data Center Growth Explains Much of the Rally

First, I think it's important to put AMD's remarkable triple-digit rally this year into context. I see two key metrics that have marked a turning point in the company's investment thesis: Data Center revenue growth and forward revenue growth.

Let's start by breaking down the first metric. Basically, the market has gone from viewing AMD as a central processing unit (CPU) manufacturer trying to gain ground in artificial intelligence (AI) graphics processing units (GPUs) to treating it as a potential second major AI infrastructure platform, behind Nvidia (NVDA).

The acceleration driven by AI demand really began to show up in AMD's results in 2026, something that wasn't nearly as pronounced in 2025. To be more specific, in the third quarter of 2025, AMD generated $4.34 billion in Data Center revenue, up 22% year-over-year. A year later, that revenue reached $8.55 billion, a 97% jump, driven by both EPYC processors, benefiting particularly from the growth of AI agents, and Instinct MI450 GPUs. As a result, Data Center now accounts for 64% of the company's total revenue, compared to less than 50% in the same period last year.

As if that weren't enough, this growth came with a considerable improvement in the segment's profitability. Data Center's operating margin rose from 25% to 34%. So, we're talking about a company whose core business has nearly doubled in size while its margins have expanded by an impressive 9 percentage points.

HSBC has identified 11 stocks it considers attractive buying opportunities following a broad market pullback, with recommendations spanning technology, industrials, energy and financial services, according to a Thursday research note.

The bank's latest selections include Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL), Applied Materials (AMAT), Baker Hughes (BKR), Bloom Energy (NYSE:BE) and Citigroup (C). The list also features Freeport-McMoRan (NYSE:FCX), GE Vernova (NYSE:GEV), NextEra Energy (NYSE:NEE), Oracle (NYSE:ORCL), Sempra (SRE) and Vertiv (VRT).

The recommendations follow a rotation that has weighed on technology and industrial shares. Both sectors have lost about 8% to 9% over the past three months, while certain industry groups have retreated nearly 20% from recent highs. HSBC views parts of the decline as excessive relative to underlying business conditions.

The bank sees potential support from artificial intelligence infrastructure spending, electricity demand, semiconductor investment and improving financial performance. Alphabet and Oracle offer exposure to AI-related cloud growth, while Applied Materials benefits from chipmaking investment. Energy and power companies could gain from rising electricity consumption and data center expansion.
